opus-5.5.text:
Well, it goes back quite a long way, really. If you look at the history of AI, there were two big traditions that grew up largely separately. One was the logical tradition: first-order logic, knowledge representation, the idea that you could describe the world in terms of objects and relations and quantify over them. You could say "every person has a mother" without enumerating every person. That gives you enormous expressive power. The other was the probabilistic tradition, which took off with Judea Pearl's work on Bayesian networks in the 1980s. That gave us a principled way to handle uncertainty, which logic struggled with.

The problem was that Bayesian networks are essentially propositional. They're like Boolean circuits: you have a fixed set of variables, and you have to write down every one of them explicitly. If you want to model a world with an unknown number of objects, or where you don't know which observation corresponds to which object, a Bayesian network just doesn't give you the vocabulary. You end up building huge, brittle models by hand, and they don't generalize.

So the motivation was to unify the two: to have the expressive power of first-order logic together with the ability to represent and reason about uncertainty. There had been earlier work on this, things like probabilistic relational models and other first-order probabilistic languages, but most of them assumed you knew exactly what objects existed and which names referred to which objects. In the real world that's almost never true. When you look at a scene, you don't know how many people are in it. When you read a set of citations, you don't know how many distinct papers or authors they refer to. When a radar picks up blips, you don't know how many aircraft there are.

BLOG, which Brian Milch and I developed along with colleagues, stands for Bayesian Logic. It was designed specifically to handle open-universe problems: unknown numbers of objects and uncertainty about identity. The model defines a probability distribution over possible worlds that can contain different sets of objects.

One application I'm particularly happy with is monitoring the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty. The problem is to take signals from a global network of seismic stations and work out what events happened: how many, where, when, and which detections correspond to which events. That's an open-universe problem. We wrote a model, NET-VISA, that was quite compact compared with the existing system, and it substantially reduced the number of missed events. I think that illustrates the point: if the language matches the structure of the problem, you can write a short, correct model and let general inference algorithms do the work.

More broadly, I've always believed that intelligent systems need to represent knowledge in a compact, compositional way, and that they need to handle uncertainty properly. I don't think either deep learning or classical logic on its own gets you all the way there, so expressive probabilistic languages are, to me, an important part of the foundation.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it really came out of a long-standing frustration with the gap between what we could say in logic and what we could reason about probabilistically. When I was a student, you had these two camps. The logical AI people could write down knowledge about objects and relations, about arbitrary numbers of things, with quantifiers, and so on. And then the probabilistic people, after Judea Pearl's work on Bayesian networks, had this beautiful machinery for handling uncertainty, but it was essentially propositional. A Bayesian network has a fixed set of variables. You have to know in advance how many things there are in the world.

And that struck me as deeply unsatisfying, because almost nothing in the real world works that way. If you're tracking aircraft on radar, you don't know how many aircraft there are. If you're trying to resolve citations in a bibliographic database, you don't know how many distinct papers or authors exist behind all those strings. The number of objects, and which observations correspond to which objects, is itself uncertain. So the uncertainty is not just about the values of some variables, it's about the structure of the world, about existence and identity.

So BLOG, Bayesian Logic, was an attempt to define a language where you could write down a generative model of the world that includes unknown numbers of objects and unknown relations between observations and objects, and then have the semantics be well-defined. That turned out to be harder than we expected, because you have to be careful about what it means to have a probability distribution over possible worlds that contain different numbers of things. Brian Milch did a lot of the heavy lifting there in his thesis.

The deeper motivation, I think, is that I've always believed that if you want to build intelligent systems, you need representations that are expressive enough to describe the world the way it actually is. The alternative, which is what a lot of the field has done, is to shrink the problem until it fits the tool. Expressive probabilistic languages let you keep the problem the way it is and build the tools up to meet it.

astra-6.text:
The motivation was to bring together two things we clearly need in AI: the ability to describe a rich, structured world, and the ability to reason under uncertainty. Logic gives us a language for talking about objects and relations, while probability theory tells us how to reason when we don’t know exactly what’s true. But many probabilistic models require you to specify the objects and variables in advance. That’s a substantial limitation, because often you don’t even know what objects exist.

Think about tracking aircraft from radar observations. You don’t know how many aircraft there are, which observations came from which aircraft, or which observations are just noise. Those aren’t peripheral uncertainties; they’re central to understanding what’s happening.

BLOG—Bayesian logic—was intended to let you describe that kind of situation naturally, including uncertainty about the number and identity of objects. You specify how the world works and how it generates observations, and then inference works backward from the observations to possible explanations. The broader aim was to make building probabilistic models much more like writing down your knowledge, with general-purpose algorithms doing the reasoning.

r002.rationale: It gives an aircraft-tracking example, but says nothing about circuit representations of game rules or their size making them implausible accounts of knowledge representation.

sol-6.1.text:
The motivation was to bring together two things we clearly needed: the expressive power of first-order logic and the ability of probability theory to handle uncertainty. A lot of probabilistic modeling began with a fixed set of variables. But in the real world, you often don’t know what objects exist, how many there are, or which observations refer to the same object. Those are things you need to reason about, not settle before you build the model.

So with BLOG—Bayesian logic—the idea was to describe a world in terms of objects, their properties and relations, while allowing uncertainty about the objects themselves. Then you could state what you knew about how the world worked and let inference work out what might be going on. The language was a way of making those models natural to express, rather than having to construct a new inference system for every problem.
